transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doctor, I... I suppose it's a long story, but my daughter insisted I come in. She drove me here this morning, actually. She's been fussing over me a lot lately, ever since her mother passed a few years back, but it's gotten worse recently. I keep telling her she has her own family to worry about, her own life, but she just won't listen. And, well, the truth is... what brings me in is that I just keep thinking my wife and the kids would be better off if I didn’t wake up. I mean, what good am I doing them now? I'm 80 years old, I'm just a burden. I sit in that house all day, staring at the walls, thinking about how much easier it would be for everyone if I just slipped away quietly in the night. It's not a passing thought, either, it's... it's heavy. It sits right here on my chest. And lately, I’ve caught myself saying out loud, even to my daughter, that I just don’t need to see another winter. The cold, the dark, the snow... I just don't have it in me anymore. I really don't. I've seen enough winters. I think it's time for me to be done.
How long have you been having these thoughts about not wanting to wake up and feeling like a burden to your family?

Well, let me think... it hasn't always been this bad, you know. I mean, missing my wife, that's been a constant ache for years, but this... this heavy feeling, this certainty that I'm just taking up space... that really started taking root after Charlie passed. Charlie was my bowling partner. We bowled together every Tuesday morning at the lanes down on 4th Street for, oh, it must have been fifteen years. He was a good man, Charlie. Always had a joke, even when his knees were giving him trouble. But then he had that stroke, and he was gone just like that. 

That was... let's see, it was just before Thanksgiving last year. So, about a year and a month ago, I suppose. After the funeral, I just couldn't bring myself to go back to the alley. I tried once, but looking at his empty chair... it just wasn't right. And that's when I started sitting in the house more. The days started bleeding into each other, and the quiet... the quiet just got so loud. That's when I started thinking about the winters, and how tired I am. It just creeps up on you, you know? One day you're having coffee with your buddy, and the next you're just waiting for the clock to run out. It's been a long year, Doctor. A very long year and a month.
Do you still find pleasure in activities you used to enjoy before your wife and Charlie passed away?

Pleasure? No... no, I really don't. I mean, I used to have a very full life, you know. I kept busy. I used to really look forward to things. Like bridge, for instance. I played bridge for decades, used to be quite sharp at it, keeping track of all the cards, anticipating what the other fellow was going to throw down. 

And my garden... oh, I had a beautiful garden out back. Grew these big beefsteak tomatoes, cucumbers, some climbing roses that my wife just adored. I'd be out there on my knees in the dirt for hours every spring and summer. It was good, honest work, pulling the weeds, feeling the sun on your back. And I used to do a lot of the cooking down at the church, too. First Presbyterian. I was the one who ran the Sunday pancake breakfasts, mixing up the batter for fifty, sixty people at a time. I had a special way of doing it with a little malt powder, and I loved seeing everyone enjoying themselves, talking over coffee. 

And the Cubs games! Lord, I’ve been a Cubs fan since I was a little boy. Used to take the train right up to Wrigley, sit in the bleachers, or at least I'd listen to every single pitch on the radio if I couldn't make it to the park. I'd keep score in a little book, inning by inning... 

But now... well, now I don't do any of that. I haven't turned a baseball game on in I don't know how long. The garden is completely overgrown with weeds, just a mess of thorns and dead vines, and I just look out the window at it and feel absolutely nothing. I don't go to the church kitchen, I don't touch a deck of cards. I just... I wake up, and I go sit in my chair in the living room. And I just sit there. All day long. The house is quiet, and I just sit in that chair, and I try to think about the things I used to love, but I just can’t make myself care about any of it anymore. The caring is just... it's just dried up. I can't make myself care.
Have you experienced any loss of interest in activities that you once found enjoyable over the past year?

Well, yes, Doctor, I... I suppose that's exactly what I was just trying to explain to you a moment ago. It's a complete loss of interest. Over this past year, especially since we lost Charlie, all of it just slipped away. 

Like I mentioned, I really used to look forward to my bridge games, tending to the garden out back, the church cooking for the Sunday breakfasts, and following my Cubs games... those were the things that gave my days a shape, you know? You'd wake up and think, 'Oh, I need to check on the tomatoes today,' or 'The Cubs are playing a double-header, better get the radio tuned.' It gave you a reason to put your shoes on. 

But now... well, as I was saying, I just sit in my chair in the living room. It's the brown recliner right by the window. I sit there and watch the dust floating in the light, and I know I should want to do something, anything, but I just can't make myself care about any of it. My daughter will even come over and ask if I want to play a hand of cards or turn the game on the television, and I just shake my head. The caring is just completely gone. So, yes, to answer your question, over the past year, I've lost interest in absolutely everything I used to enjoy. I just sit in that chair.
Have you thought about how you would end your life if you decided to go through with it?

Well... how I'd do it? I... I don't know that I have a grand plan, Doctor. It's not like I'm sitting in that brown recliner drawing up blueprints or hoarding pills in the medicine cabinet. It's more of a... a quiet wish, I suppose. 

Like I was saying earlier, what really brought me in here, what my daughter was so worried about, is that I just keep thinking that she, and her brother, and everyone else... they would all just be so much better off if I didn't wake up in the morning. I go to sleep in that big empty bed, and I just pray, I really do, I pray to the good Lord that I just slip away in the night. No fuss, no mess for the kids to clean up. Just... done. 

And lately, well, I've been saying it out loud, which I know upsets them, but it's the truth... I've been telling them I don't need to see another winter. The winters here, they're so long, and the cold just gets right into your bones, especially at my age. The ice on the sidewalks, the gray skies that just hang there for months... I just can't face it again. I don't want to see another snowstorm. I just want to close my eyes and be with my wife. So, no, no specific method, no gun or rope or anything violent like that. Just... hoping the clock stops ticking. Just hoping I don't have to see another winter.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?

Weight? Well, I... I don't really know for sure, Doctor. I haven't been on a scale in, oh, I couldn't tell you how long. My wife, she used to keep a little white scale in the bathroom, right next to the laundry hamper, and she'd step on it every Sunday morning before church, but me, I never paid it much mind. 

I suppose my clothes are fitting a bit looser these days. The trousers I wear, the khaki ones I usually put on in the morning when I get out of bed to go sit in my chair, they seem to bag a little around the waist. I've had to pull my belt a notch tighter, maybe two. And my collars, they feel a bit roomy on my neck. 

But as for a significant amount, like a specific number of pounds? I just couldn't say. I haven't been paying attention to numbers. I just... I don't eat much anymore, I suppose. Like I said before, I used to love cooking down at the church, the pancake breakfasts, and I used to enjoy a good meal. My wife was a wonderful cook, made a pot roast that would just melt in your mouth, with the carrots and the little red potatoes... 

But now, food just tastes like cardboard. I'll make a piece of toast in the morning, maybe have a cup of tea, and half the time the toast just sits there on the plate getting cold while I look out the window at the dead vines in the garden. My daughter brings over casseroles, leaves them in the fridge with little sticky notes on them, telling me to heat them up at 350 degrees for twenty minutes. I know she means well, bless her heart, she's trying so hard, but I just can't bring myself to eat them. I'll take a bite or two just so I can tell her I did, but I have no appetite. None at all. So, I imagine I must have lost some weight, given how my trousers are hanging on me, but I couldn't give you an exact figure, Doctor. I just don't know.
Have you thought about a specific way you would end your life if you decided to go through with it?

Well, Doctor, I... I feel like we might be going in circles a bit here, because I think I just tried to explain this to you a moment ago, but maybe I didn't make myself clear enough. My hearing isn't what it used to be, but I'm pretty sure I don't have a specific... a particular method picked out. No guns, no standing on bridges. 

It's really just exactly what brings me in here today in the first place. I just keep thinking my wife and the kids would be better off if I didn’t wake up. I know I mentioned wanting to be with my wife earlier, and sometimes things get a little... a little muddled in my head these days. Sometimes I swear I can hear her right upstairs making the bed or humming in the kitchen, and it feels like she's still here worrying about me just like the kids do. But whether she's in the next room or up in heaven, I just know they'd all be so much better off without me dragging them down. 

My daughter coming over with those casseroles I can't eat, my son always calling to check if I've left the stove on... it's just too much of a burden on everyone. I'm just taking up space in that brown recliner. And lately, well, I’ve been saying I don’t need to see another winter. I've been saying it right out loud to them. I look out that front window, and I start thinking about how the ice is going to coat the branches of the old oak tree out there, and how the wind always howls through the storm windows in January, making the whole house drafty... and I just don't want any part of it anymore. 

I'm just tired, Doctor. Deep down in my bones tired. So, no, I don't have a blueprint for doing anything drastic. I just go to bed praying I don't open my eyes when the morning comes. I just want to slip away quietly before the snow flies.
Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Well, moving slowly... yes, I suppose I do. It’s funny you ask that, because just the other day, my wife—well, I know she’s gone, but I could swear I heard her voice clear as a bell from the hallway—she said to me, "You move like you’re walking through deep snow." And she’s right, she really is. It’s like... like my legs are made of lead, or like I'm trying to wade through a snowdrift that's up to my waist. Every step is just such an effort. 

It used to be I could hop out of bed, get my trousers on, shave, and be down in the kitchen putting the kettle on before the sun was fully up. But now? Now, just getting out from under the covers feels like a chore I can barely manage. Getting dressed takes me forever. I’ll sit on the edge of the bed with one sock in my hand for... I don't know, twenty minutes, just staring at the floorboards, trying to gather the energy to bend over and put it on my foot. 

And crossing the kitchen... it feels like walking a mile. I'll get up from my chair in the living room, thinking maybe I'll go get a glass of water or see if there's any tea left in the pot, and by the time I make it halfway across the linoleum, I'm just so exhausted. I just stop right there in the middle of the room. It takes so long to do the simplest things that most of the time, I just give up. I just turn around, shuffle back to my recliner, and sit back down. It’s just not worth the effort anymore. Even talking feels like a strain sometimes, like I have to search for the words and drag them up from somewhere deep down. Everything is just so heavy, Doctor. So terribly heavy.
Do you often feel guilty or worthless about your current situation or the things you've done in the past?

Guilty? Oh... oh, Doctor, if you only knew. When you sit in a brown recliner all day long, just staring at the dust motes floating in the sunlight by the window, your mind... well, it goes to some dark places. You have nothing but time to look back. And I just... I keep going over every little thing I did wrong. Every single mistake. 

Especially with my son. I think about all the times I was too hard on him when he was a boy, or the times I worked late instead of coming home for dinner, or how I snapped at him over something foolish like leaving his bicycle in the driveway. I replay it all in my head, over and over, like a broken record. With him, and with my whole family. My wife, my daughter... I failed them. I really did. I thought I was doing right by them back then, but I wasn't. I missed so much, and I made so many wrong turns. 

And now look at me. My daughter has to bring me food I can't even chew, my son has to call and make sure I haven't burned the house down... I feel like I’m just absolutely no good to anybody anymore. I'm worse than useless, Doctor. I'm a drain on the people who are supposed to be living their own lives. 

And to tell you the truth, when I really sit and think about it... I feel like I deserve this. All this misery, this terrible heaviness... I deserve whatever punishment is coming to me. Sometimes I think that's why I hear my wife's voice in the hall, you know? She's a reminder of all my sins, of all the ways I fell short as a husband and a father. I've got a punishment coming, whether it's in this life or the next, and I just have to sit here and take it, because I know I've earned every bit of it.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or having trouble sitting still, or is it more that you feel slowed down and have trouble getting started on things?

Well, Doctor, I... I thought we just talked about this, didn't we? Or maybe I didn't explain it right. My memory gets a little fuzzy these days, but I could have sworn I just told you about how hard it is to get moving. 

Restless? No, no, it's nothing like that. I'm not pacing the floors or wringing my hands or anything of the sort. It's quite the opposite, really. Like I said before, it's just this terrible, overwhelming slowness. I'm just so slowed down. I told you about what my wife said, right? I know she passed on, but I still hear her sometimes, and she told me, "You move like you're walking through deep snow." And she hit the nail right on the head. That's exactly what it feels like. 

Every little thing is just... it's just a monumental task. I mean, just the other morning—or maybe it was last week, the days all run together now—I woke up and thought, 'Alright, time to get up and put on a clean shirt.' Just a simple thing, right? Something I've done every day of my life for eighty years. But I sat there on the edge of the mattress, looking at the closet door, and it just felt like it was miles away. My arms and legs felt so heavy, like they were made of solid lead. I must have sat there for half an hour just staring at my slippers, trying to figure out how to make my body do what I wanted it to do. 

And it's the same thing when I try to do anything else. I told you about trying to get across the kitchen, didn't I? I get halfway to the sink to get a glass of water, and it takes so much effort, so much energy just to lift my feet and put them down again, that I just... I just stop. I give up before I've even done much of anything. I just turn around and shuffle all the way back to my recliner and sit back down. It's just not worth the struggle. So, no, I'm certainly not restless. I'm just stuck. Stuck in this awful, heavy slowness.
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that aren't there when you're alone?

Voices... well, yes. I... I think I mentioned my wife earlier, didn't I? Hearing her out in the hall. But it's... it's not just her. It's my son, too. And that's the one that really just tears me apart. 

You see, in the evenings, when the sun starts going down and the shadows get long across the living room carpet... I just sit there in my recliner. It gets so quiet you can hear the grandfather clock ticking out in the dining room. But then, out of nowhere, I hear his voice. My son's voice. Some evenings I hear his voice plain as day from the hallway, or sometimes it comes from the spare room—the one that used to be his bedroom when he was just a little boy, before he grew up and moved away. 

He's not a little boy when I hear him now, though. It's his grown-up voice. And he's... he's telling me I should have been there. He tells me that I failed him. It echoes right out of that spare room: 'You weren't there, Dad. You failed me.' Over and over. And the words just hit me like a physical blow, because, like I was saying before, I know he's right. I know I made so many mistakes with him. I replay them all day long, and then at night, he's right there in the house saying them out loud to me. 

And the most confusing part, Doctor... the part that really makes my head spin... is that sometimes my wife is sitting right there with me. I know she passed on, I know that in my head, but she's there, and I'll look at her and ask if she heard him. But even when my wife says the house is quiet... even when she tells me it's just the two of us and there's not a sound... I still hear him. I hear him judging me. Condemning me. I hear it so clearly, even when she promises me the house is completely quiet. I just sit there in the dusk, listening to him tell me what a terrible father I was, because... well, because I don't have the energy to get up and close the door, and because I know I deserve to hear every single word of it.
Do you feel like you're moving more quickly than usual or have extra energy?

Moving quickly? Extra energy? Doctor, I... I'm sorry, but are you sure you're listening to me? I feel like we're just going around in circles here. I... I know my memory isn't what it used to be, but I'm absolutely certain I just explained this to you a few minutes ago. 

There is no extra energy. None whatsoever. It's... it's just the exact opposite. Like I told you before, my wife says I move like I’m walking through deep snow. And she's right. You know that heavy, wet snow that just packs around your boots and drags you down with every single step, making your legs ache? That's my whole life now. That's every hour of every day. 

Moving quickly is completely out of the question. I mean, I already told you about the mornings, didn't I? Just the simple act of getting dressed, trying to put my arms through the sleeves of a shirt... or trying to cross the kitchen floor just to get to the sink. It takes me so long, and requires so much sheer willpower just to lift my feet off the linoleum, that I just give up before I’ve done much of anything at all. The energy it takes just to stand there... it drains whatever little bit of life I have left in me. I just turn around and go back to my chair. So, no. No extra energy, Doctor. I couldn't move quickly if the house was on fire.
Have you thought about a specific way you would end your life if you decided to go through with it, beyond just hoping not to wake up?

A specific way? Well, Doctor, I... I don't know about a specific way, like doing something violent or... or making some big elaborate plan. Like I just tried to explain, I don't have the energy to even cross the kitchen floor to get a glass of water, so how could I possibly manage to carry out anything complicated? But... but the thoughts are there. They are always there, pressing down on me, heavy as lead. 

Actually, it is the main reason I am even talking to you today. What really brings me in is... well, I just keep thinking my wife and the kids would be better off if I didn't wake up. I know I mentioned my wife passing on, but with her still sitting there in the room with me in the evenings, and my son's voice echoing down the hall telling me what a failure I am... I just feel the weight of what a terrible disappointment I am to all of them. I am just a useless old man taking up space in that recliner. If I just went to sleep tonight and my heart simply stopped, it would be a mercy. A mercy for them, mostly. They would finally be free of my mistakes.

And lately... lately I have been looking out the window at the yard, watching the days get shorter, and I have been saying I don't need to see another winter. I really don't. The winters get so terribly bitter in that old house, and the drafts come right through the living room windows. I just sit there shivering because I can't even gather the strength to get up and adjust the thermostat. I just sit there and think about the frost on the glass and the snow piling up outside, and I tell myself, I don't need to endure another season of this. I don't need to see another winter at all. If the cold just settled into my bones one night and I drifted off for good... well, that would just be the best thing for everyone. My son wouldn't have to yell at me from the spare room anymore. The house could just finally be at peace. So no, I don't have the energy to do anything to myself, I just... I just want to close my eyes and let that be the end of it.
Have you lost more than 5% of your body weight over the past year?

Weight? Oh, well... I couldn't say for sure about percentages or anything like that. I don't own a scale anymore. My wife used to have one of those old dial scales in the bathroom, the kind with the little red needle, but I think it broke years ago and we just never replaced it. So I don't have a number to give you, Doctor. 

But... well, I suppose I have noticed my clothes don't fit right anymore. My trousers, the ones I've worn for years, they just hang off me now. I have to pull my belt tight, to the very last notch, and even then, they bunch up all around my waist. It's like I'm shrinking away to nothing. And my shirts... the collars are so loose on my neck. I feel like a scarecrow sitting in that recliner. 

But I don't know if it's 5 percent or 10 percent or what. I just know that I don't have the appetite I used to. I don't have the energy to cook, of course, like I was telling you about just getting across the kitchen. So I just don't eat much. A piece of toast maybe, if I can manage it. But mostly I just sit there and watch the clock, and the weight just seems to be slipping away on its own, just like everything else. So, I don't know the exact amount, Doctor, I really don't, but yes, I'm definitely smaller than I was last year.
For how long have you felt no interest in the things you used to enjoy?

Interest in things? Well, Doctor... it's been a long time. A very long time. It feels like an eternity, really, sitting in that chair every single day. But if I had to put a date on it, if I really had to trace it back to when the color just completely drained out of everything... it would be when Arthur passed away. 

Arthur was my bowling partner. We bowled together every Tuesday and Thursday morning down at the lanes on Elm Street. We had this routine, you see. We'd get there at 9:00 AM sharp, get our shoes, drink a cup of that terrible burnt coffee they serve at the concession stand, and bowl three games. We weren't very good anymore, mostly throwing gutter balls with our arthritis, but... but it was something to do. It was a reason to leave the house. 

He died... let's see, it was just over a year ago. A year and a month ago, to be exact. It was a Tuesday, actually. I was waiting for him at the lanes, and he never showed up. His daughter called me later that afternoon to tell me his heart just gave out in his sleep. 

And ever since that day, Doctor... ever since that phone call a year and a month ago, I haven't been back to the alley. I haven't taken my bowling ball out of the bag in the closet. I haven't even wanted to. My wife kept telling me I should go back, find a new partner, or just bowl on my own to get out of the house. But what's the point? Without Arthur there to complain about the waxed floors or the noisy kids in the next lane... there's just no joy in it. There's no joy in anything anymore. Not bowling, not watching the baseball games on television, not even reading the morning paper. It all just stopped meaning anything when he died. So, yes, it's been about a year and a month of just... nothing. Just sitting and waiting.
Have you ever seen things that aren't there when you're alone, like shadows or movements out of the corner of your eye?

Shadows? Movements? Well... no, Doctor, I wouldn't say I see shadows or things darting around, no. My eyesight isn't what it used to be, of course, with the cataracts and all, but... but it's not my eyes that are the problem. It's... it's what I hear. 

I know I mentioned my son earlier, how he yells at me from the spare room. Some evenings, when I'm just sitting there in the recliner, the house gets so terribly quiet. You know that kind of quiet where the silence almost rings in your ears? That's when it happens. I'll be sitting there, maybe dozing off a bit, and then... I hear his voice. Plain as day, Doctor. It's not a whisper, it's not a trick of the wind. It's him. He's standing right down the hallway, or sometimes he's just inside the spare room with the door cracked open, and he's talking to me. 

He tells me... well, he tells me I should have been there for him. He tells me what a failure I am, how I ruined everything, how I let everyone down. The things he says, they cut right through me. And the tone of his voice, it's so full of disappointment and anger. It's exactly how he sounded that day he left for good, years ago. 

And the strangest part is... my wife, she'll be sitting right there in the living room with me, knitting or just staring out the window, and she doesn't hear a thing. I'll look over at her and say, 'Did you hear what he just said?' And she'll just shake her head, looking at me with this... this pity in her eyes, and she'll tell me the house is completely quiet. She tells me nobody is there, that it's just the two of us. But how can she not hear it? It echoes down the hall. It fills the whole room. 

So no, I don't see shadows creeping around the corners, Doctor. But the voices... his voice... it's there. It's so real I could just get up and walk down the hall and find him, if I only had the energy to get out of the chair. But I don't. So I just sit there and listen to him tell me what a terrible father I was, while my wife insists the house is empty.
Do you have a specific plan in mind for how you would end your life if you decided to go through with it?

A specific plan... well, Doctor, I don't know if you would call it a plan, exactly. It's not like I've gone out and bought a rope or... or hoarded away a bunch of pills in the medicine cabinet. I don't have the energy for all that plotting and scheming anyway. I can barely make it across the kitchen, let alone orchestrate something complicated. 

But... well, what actually brings me in here, what finally made my wife insist I come sit in this office and talk to you, is what I've been saying around the house lately. I just... I keep thinking that my wife and the kids, they would all be so much better off if I simply didn't wake up. Just went to sleep in that recliner and that was the end of it. No fuss, no mess. Because right now, I'm just an anchor around their necks, aren't I? Just a frail old man sitting in the quiet, listening to his son's voice tell him what a failure he is. They shouldn't have to deal with that. It's not fair to my wife, having to watch me shrink away to nothing. 

And lately... well, I've been looking out that front window, watching the leaves, feeling that chill creeping into the morning air. And I've been saying to her, just right out loud... I tell her I don't need to see another winter. I really don't. The winters here, they're so incredibly long and bitter, and the cold just seeps right into my bones, right into my joints where the arthritis is already so bad. But it's more than just the physical cold, Doctor. It's the darkness. The sun sets so early, and the house gets so terribly dark and empty. 

I just... I don't want to be here for it. I don't need to see the snow fall again. I don't want to sit in that chair and watch another year freeze over. So, a plan? Maybe I don't have a step-by-step instruction manual drawn up, but... I just want to close my eyes and drift off before the first hard freeze comes. That's what I want. They would all just be so much better off if I slipped away in my sleep before December gets here.
For how long have you felt no interest in the things you used to enjoy?

Well, Doctor, I... I thought we just went over this, didn't we? Or maybe all these questions are just blending together in my head. My memory isn't quite what it used to be, but I'm fairly certain I was just telling you about Arthur. But... well, to answer you again, just to be clear, it's been about a year and a month. A year and a month exactly, since my bowling partner passed away. 

That was the turning point, you see. That was when it all just stopped. Before that, even with the arthritis acting up and my knees getting so stiff in the mornings, I still had a reason to get up, put on my shoes, and head down to the lanes on Elm Street. We had our routine, Tuesday and Thursday mornings, like clockwork. But since his daughter called me that afternoon... since I found out his heart just gave out in his sleep... the color just completely drained right out of my life. 

So, yes, it's been about thirteen months of this. This has been going on since Arthur died, a year and a month ago. A year and a month of just sitting in my recliner, watching the dust motes float in the air while my wife tries to hand me the morning paper. She'll say to me, she'll say I should look at the baseball scores, or she'll suggest I go down to the alley and just watch the others bowl, just to get out of the house. But I have absolutely no desire to. None at all. Not for bowling, not for reading, not for watching the television. It all just stopped mattering a year and a month ago when I lost him. That's exactly how long this... this total lack of interest has been going on. Just nothing but sitting and waiting since then.
Have you ever seen or heard things that you know are not real, when you are alone or even when you are with other people?

Well, Doctor, I... I feel like we might be going in circles just a bit here. Didn't I just tell you about this when I first sat down? About my son? 

I know you doctors have a checklist of questions you have to get through, and my memory isn't perfect these days, but I'm quite sure I already explained about the spare room. But, well, to answer you again... yes. I don't see things, I already told you that, but I do hear him. 

It happens on those evenings when the house settles and the television is off. I'll be in my chair, and then I hear his voice, plain as day. It comes right down the hallway, or sometimes it sounds like it's drifting out from the spare room where he used to sleep. And he's so angry, Doctor. He's telling me that I should have been there for him. He tells me over and over that I failed him, that I was a terrible father. It's a heavy thing to listen to, just sitting there in the dim light, having your past thrown right in your face like that. 

And like I mentioned before, the part that makes me feel like I'm losing my grip is my wife. She'll be sitting right there in the very same room, not ten feet away from me. And the Cubs games! Lord, I’ve been a Cubs fan since I was a little boy. Used to take the train right up to Wrigley, sit in the bleachers, or at least I'd listen to every single pitch on the radio if I couldn't make it to the park. I'd keep score in a little book, inning by inning...

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost more than 5% of your body weight over the past year?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about weight loss, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Weight? Oh, well... I couldn't say for sure about percentages or anything like that. I don't own a scale anymore. My wife used to have one of those old dial scales in the bathroom, the kind with the little red needle, but I think it broke years ago and we just never replaced it. So I don't have a number to give you, Doctor. 

But... well, I suppose I have noticed my clothes don't fit right anymore. My trousers, the ones I've worn for years, they just hang off me now. I have to pull my belt tight, to the very last notch, and even then, they bunch up all around my waist. It's like I'm shrinking away to nothing. And my shirts... the collars are so loose on my neck. I feel like a scarecrow sitting in that recliner. 

But I don't know if it's 5 percent or 10 percent or what. I just know that I don't have the appetite I used to. I don't have the energy to cook, of course, like I was telling you about just getting across the kitchen. So I just don't eat much. A piece of toast maybe, if I can manage it. But mostly I just sit there and watch the clock, and the weight just seems to be slipping away on its own, just like everything else. So, I don't know the exact amount, Doctor, I really don't, but yes, I'm definitely smaller than I was last year.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's loss of interest in activities
doctor.question: For how long have you felt no interest in the things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since my bowling partner died, about a year and a month ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for the timeframe or duration of the patient's symptoms (specifically the loss of interest).

patient.answer:
Interest in things? Well, Doctor... it's been a long time. A very long time. It feels like an eternity, really, sitting in that chair every single day. But if I had to put a date on it, if I really had to trace it back to when the color just completely drained out of everything... it would be when Arthur passed away. 

Arthur was my bowling partner. We bowled together every Tuesday and Thursday morning down at the lanes on Elm Street. We had this routine, you see. We'd get there at 9:00 AM sharp, get our shoes, drink a cup of that terrible burnt coffee they serve at the concession stand, and bowl three games. We weren't very good anymore, mostly throwing gutter balls with our arthritis, but... but it was something to do. It was a reason to leave the house. 

He died... let's see, it was just over a year ago. A year and a month ago, to be exact. It was a Tuesday, actually. I was waiting for him at the lanes, and he never showed up. His daughter called me later that afternoon to tell me his heart just gave out in his sleep. 

And ever since that day, Doctor... ever since that phone call a year and a month ago, I haven't been back to the alley. I haven't taken my bowling ball out of the bag in the closet. I haven't even wanted to. My wife kept telling me I should go back, find a new partner, or just bowl on my own to get out of the house. But what's the point? Without Arthur there to complain about the waxed floors or the noisy kids in the next lane... there's just no joy in it. There's no joy in anything anymore. Not bowling, not watching the baseball games on television, not even reading the morning paper. It all just stopped meaning anything when he died. So, yes, it's been about a year and a month of just... nothing. Just sitting and waiting.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you ever seen things that aren't there when you're alone, like shadows or movements out of the corner of your eye?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Some evenings I hear his voice plain as day from the hallway or the spare room, telling me I should have been there or that I failed him, even when my wife says the house is quiet.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about seeing things that aren't there, which relates to the symptom of hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Shadows? Movements? Well... no, Doctor, I wouldn't say I see shadows or things darting around, no. My eyesight isn't what it used to be, of course, with the cataracts and all, but... but it's not my eyes that are the problem. It's... it's what I hear. 

I know I mentioned my son earlier, how he yells at me from the spare room. Some evenings, when I'm just sitting there in the recliner, the house gets so terribly quiet. You know that kind of quiet where the silence almost rings in your ears? That's when it happens. I'll be sitting there, maybe dozing off a bit, and then... I hear his voice. Plain as day, Doctor. It's not a whisper, it's not a trick of the wind. It's him. He's standing right down the hallway, or sometimes he's just inside the spare room with the door cracked open, and he's talking to me. 

He tells me... well, he tells me I should have been there for him. He tells me what a failure I am, how I ruined everything, how I let everyone down. The things he says, they cut right through me. And the tone of his voice, it's so full of disappointment and anger. It's exactly how he sounded that day he left for good, years ago. 

And the strangest part is... my wife, she'll be sitting right there in the living room with me, knitting or just staring out the window, and she doesn't hear a thing. I'll look over at her and say, 'Did you hear what he just said?' And she'll just shake her head, looking at me with this... this pity in her eyes, and she'll tell me the house is completely quiet. She tells me nobody is there, that it's just the two of us. But how can she not hear it? It echoes down the hall. It fills the whole room. 

So no, I don't see shadows creeping around the corners, Doctor. But the voices... his voice... it's there. It's so real I could just get up and walk down the hall and find him, if I only had the energy to get out of the chair. But I don't. So I just sit there and listen to him tell me what a terrible father I was, while my wife insists the house is empty.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has suicidal intent with a plan
doctor.question: Do you have a specific plan in mind for how you would end your life if you decided to go through with it?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I keep thinking my wife and the kids would be better off if I didn’t wake up, and lately I’ve been saying I don’t need to see another winter.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal plans, which corresponds to the Death_Suicide symptom profile.

patient.answer:
A specific plan... well, Doctor, I don't know if you would call it a plan, exactly. It's not like I've gone out and bought a rope or... or hoarded away a bunch of pills in the medicine cabinet. I don't have the energy for all that plotting and scheming anyway. I can barely make it across the kitchen, let alone orchestrate something complicated. 

But... well, what actually brings me in here, what finally made my wife insist I come sit in this office and talk to you, is what I've been saying around the house lately. I just... I keep thinking that my wife and the kids, they would all be so much better off if I simply didn't wake up. Just went to sleep in that recliner and that was the end of it. No fuss, no mess. Because right now, I'm just an anchor around their necks, aren't I? Just a frail old man sitting in the quiet, listening to his son's voice tell him what a failure he is. They shouldn't have to deal with that. It's not fair to my wife, having to watch me shrink away to nothing. 

And lately... well, I've been looking out that front window, watching the leaves, feeling that chill creeping into the morning air. And I've been saying to her, just right out loud... I tell her I don't need to see another winter. I really don't. The winters here, they're so incredibly long and bitter, and the cold just seeps right into my bones, right into my joints where the arthritis is already so bad. But it's more than just the physical cold, Doctor. It's the darkness. The sun sets so early, and the house gets so terribly dark and empty. 

I just... I don't want to be here for it. I don't need to see the snow fall again. I don't want to sit in that chair and watch another year freeze over. So, a plan? Maybe I don't have a step-by-step instruction manual drawn up, but... I just want to close my eyes and drift off before the first hard freeze comes. That's what I want. They would all just be so much better off if I slipped away in my sleep before December gets here.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's loss of interest in activities
doctor.question: For how long have you felt no interest in the things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since my bowling partner died, about a year and a month ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking 'For how long', which corresponds to the duration of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, Doctor, I... I thought we just went over this, didn't we? Or maybe all these questions are just blending together in my head. My memory isn't quite what it used to be, but I'm fairly certain I was just telling you about Arthur. But... well, to answer you again, just to be clear, it's been about a year and a month. A year and a month exactly, since my bowling partner passed away. 

That was the turning point, you see. That was when it all just stopped. Before that, even with the arthritis acting up and my knees getting so stiff in the mornings, I still had a reason to get up, put on my shoes, and head down to the lanes on Elm Street. We had our routine, Tuesday and Thursday mornings, like clockwork. But since his daughter called me that afternoon... since I found out his heart just gave out in his sleep... the color just completely drained right out of my life. 

So, yes, it's been about thirteen months of this. This has been going on since Arthur died, a year and a month ago. A year and a month of just sitting in my recliner, watching the dust motes float in the air while my wife tries to hand me the morning paper. She'll say to me, she'll say I should look at the baseball scores, or she'll suggest I go down to the alley and just watch the others bowl, just to get out of the house. But I have absolutely no desire to. None at all. Not for bowling, not for reading, not for watching the television. It all just stopped mattering a year and a month ago when I lost him. That's exactly how long this... this total lack of interest has been going on. Just nothing but sitting and waiting since then.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you ever seen or heard things that you know are not real, when you are alone or even when you are with other people?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Some evenings I hear his voice plain as day from the hallway or the spare room, telling me I should have been there or that I failed him, even when my wife says the house is quiet.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about seeing or hearing things that are not real, which directly refers to hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Well, Doctor, I... I feel like we might be going in circles just a bit here. Didn't I just tell you about this when I first sat down? About my son? 

I know you doctors have a checklist of questions you have to get through, and my memory isn't perfect these days, but I'm quite sure I already explained about the spare room. But, well, to answer you again... yes. I don't see things, I already told you that, but I do hear him. 

It happens on those evenings when the house settles and the television is off. I'll be in my chair, and then I hear his voice, plain as day. It comes right down the hallway, or sometimes it sounds like it's drifting out from the spare room where he used to sleep. And he's so angry, Doctor. He's telling me that I should have been there for him. He tells me over and over that I failed him, that I was a terrible father. It's a heavy thing to listen to, just sitting there in the dim light, having your past thrown right in your face like that. 

And like I mentioned before, the part that makes me feel like I'm losing my grip is my wife. She'll be sitting right there in the very same room, not ten feet away from me. I'll hear him so clearly, and I'll look over at her, expecting her to say something, but she'll just be turning the page of her book. When I ask her about it, she just looks at me with those sad eyes and says the house is completely quiet. She swears up and down there's no one there but us. 

So, you ask if I hear things that aren't real. My wife says they aren't real. She says the house is empty. But I'm telling you, Doctor, when I hear him telling me I failed him, it's as real to me as the sound of your voice right now. I just don't understand how she can't hear it when it echoes right down the hall.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a depressive episode for more than two weeks
doctor.question: Have you felt this way, with no interest in things and feeling heavy, for more than two weeks at any point?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My wife says I move like I’m walking through deep snow, and even getting dressed or crossing the kitchen takes me so long that I give up before I’ve done much of anything.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question mentions 'feeling heavy', which directly relates to the patient's psychomotor retardation (moving like walking through deep snow).

patient.answer:
More than two weeks? Oh, Doctor, yes. I... I thought I made that clear when we were talking about Arthur a moment ago. It's been every single day for a year and a month. There hasn't been a single day in all that time where this feeling has lifted. Not one. 

And when you use that word, heavy... well, you've hit the nail right on the head. It's a terrible, physical weight. It's not just in my head, it's deep in my bones. My wife, she watches me try to get up in the mornings, and she says I move like I’m walking through deep snow. That's exactly how she describes it to me. Like I'm trudging through a heavy, wet blizzard just to get across the room. The arthritis doesn't help, of course, but it's so much more than just stiff joints. It's this absolute, total drain on my entire body. 

Just the simple act of getting dressed... I'll sit on the edge of the mattress with a sock in my hand, just staring at the floor, because the sheer effort required to bend over and pull it on feels impossible. And crossing the kitchen? Just trying to make it from the hallway to the sink to fetch a simple glass of water takes me so terribly long now. The linoleum feels like it stretches on for miles. It takes so much out of me just putting one foot in front of the other that, most of the time, I just give up before I’ve done much of anything at all. I just abandon the idea of the water or the clothes and turn right back around to sink into my recliner. 

So, yes, two weeks is just a drop in the bucket, Doctor. It's been over a year of wading through this deep snow, day in and day out, with no end in sight.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a persistent loss of interest in activities that once brought pleasure, significant weight loss, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and recurrent thoughts of death, which have been present for more than two weeks, indicating a Major Depressive Disorder.
